claim: The increasing incidence of anxiety-related disorders calls for a better understanding of anxiety- and stress-related processes.
source: The increasing incidence (e.g., Xiong et al., 2022) and high relapse rates (Essau et al., 2018; Yonkers et al., 2003) of anxiety-related disorders call for a better understanding of anxiety- and stress-related processes which might contribute to improving existing treatments or developing more effective interventions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Xiong et al., 2022; Essau et al., 2018; and Yonkers et al., 2003

claim: Anxiety-related disorders have high relapse rates.
source: The increasing incidence (e.g., Xiong et al., 2022) and high relapse rates (Essau et al., 2018; Yonkers et al., 2003) of anxiety-related disorders call for a better understanding of anxiety- and stress-related processes which might contribute to improving existing treatments or developing more effective interventions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Essau et al., 2018 and Yonkers et al., 2003

claim: Anxiety- and stress-related processes can be studied in the laboratory using fear conditioning paradigms.
source: In the laboratory, these processes can be studied using fear conditioning paradigms (Dunsmoor et al., 2022; Fullana et al., 2020; Milad and Quirk, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dunsmoor et al., 2022; Fullana et al., 2020; and Milad and Quirk, 2012

claim: In differential fear conditioning protocols, one stimulus is repetitively paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus and becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS+).
source: In differential fear conditioning protocols (see Lonsdorf et al., 2017a) one stimulus is repetitively paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US; e.g., electrotactile stimulation), and as a consequence becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS+) while another stimulus, the CS−, is never paired with the US.
evidence: Describes the standard differential fear conditioning protocol with citation to Lonsdorf et al., 2017a

claim: Another stimulus (CS−) is never paired with the US in differential fear conditioning protocols.
source: In differential fear conditioning protocols (see Lonsdorf et al., 2017a) one stimulus is repetitively paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US; e.g., electrotactile stimulation), and as a consequence becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS+) while another stimulus, the CS−, is never paired with the US.
evidence: Describes the standard differential fear conditioning protocol with citation to Lonsdorf et al., 2017a

claim: Presenting CSs without the US during extinction training leads to a gradual waning of the conditioned response.
source: After this acquisition training phase, CSs are presented without the US (extinction training) leading to a gradual waning of the conditioned response.
evidence: Describes the extinction training process based on established knowledge in the field

claim: The fear memory (CS+/US association) is not erased during extinction training.
source: Critically, the fear memory (CS+/US association) is not erased, but a competing inhibitory extinction memory (CS+/no US association) is assumed to be formed during extinction training (Milad and Quirk, 2012; Myers and Davis, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milad and Quirk, 2012 and Myers and Davis, 2007

claim: A competing inhibitory extinction memory (CS+/no US association) is assumed to be formed during extinction training.
source: Critically, the fear memory (CS+/US association) is not erased, but a competing inhibitory extinction memory (CS+/no US association) is assumed to be formed during extinction training (Milad and Quirk, 2012; Myers and Davis, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milad and Quirk, 2012 and Myers and Davis, 2007

claim: Return of fear can be induced by a time delay (spontaneous recovery).
source: Subsequently, return of fear (RoF) can be induced by procedural manipulations such as a time delay (spontaneous recovery), a contextual change (renewal, Vervliet et al., 2013a), or a (re-)presentation of an aversive event (reinstatement, Haaker et al., 2014).
evidence: Describes return of fear mechanisms based on established knowledge

claim: Return of fear can be induced by a contextual change (renewal).
source: Subsequently, return of fear (RoF) can be induced by procedural manipulations such as a time delay (spontaneous recovery), a contextual change (renewal, Vervliet et al., 2013a), or a (re-)presentation of an aversive event (reinstatement, Haaker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vervliet et al., 2013a

claim: Return of fear can be induced by a (re-)presentation of an aversive event (reinstatement).
source: Subsequently, return of fear (RoF) can be induced by procedural manipulations such as a time delay (spontaneous recovery), a contextual change (renewal, Vervliet et al., 2013a), or a (re-)presentation of an aversive event (reinstatement, Haaker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haaker et al., 2014

claim: Findings from fear conditioning paradigms hold strong potential for translating neuroscientific findings into clinical applications.
source: Findings from studies employing fear conditioning paradigms hold strong potential for translating neuroscientific findings into clinical applications (Anderson and Insel, 2006; Cooper et al., 2022a; Fullana et al., 2020; Milad and Quirk, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson and Insel, 2006; Cooper et al., 2022a; Fullana et al., 2020; and Milad and Quirk, 2012

claim: Extinction learning is assumed to be the active component of exposure-based treatment.
source: More precisely, extinction learning is assumed to be the active component of exposure-based treatment (Graham and Milad, 2011; Milad and Quirk, 2012; Rachman, 1989; Vervliet et al., 2013b) and experimental RoF manipulations have been suggested to serve as a model of clinical relapse (Scharfenort et al., 2016; Vervliet et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Graham and Milad, 2011; Milad and Quirk, 2012; Rachman, 1989; and Vervliet et al., 2013b

claim: Experimental return of fear manipulations have been suggested to serve as a model of clinical relapse.
source: More precisely, extinction learning is assumed to be the active component of exposure-based treatment (Graham and Milad, 2011; Milad and Quirk, 2012; Rachman, 1989; Vervliet et al., 2013b) and experimental RoF manipulations have been suggested to serve as a model of clinical relapse (Scharfenort et al., 2016; Vervliet et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scharfenort et al., 2016 and Vervliet et al., 2013a

claim: Patients suffering from anxiety-related disorders show deficient learning of the safety signal (CS−) during acquisition training compared to healthy controls.
source: Important findings in the fear conditioning field include the deficient learning of the safety signal (CS−) during acquisition training, impaired extinction learning (Duits et al., 2015) and the tendency of fear generalization to innocuous stimuli (Cooper et al., 2022a) in patients suffering from anxiety-related disorders as compared to healthy controls.
evidence: Describes findings in the fear conditioning field

claim: Patients suffering from anxiety-related disorders show impaired extinction learning compared to healthy controls.
source: Important findings in the fear conditioning field include the deficient learning of the safety signal (CS−) during acquisition training, impaired extinction learning (Duits et al., 2015) and the tendency of fear generalization to innocuous stimuli (Cooper et al., 2022a) in patients suffering from anxiety-related disorders as compared to healthy controls.
evidence: Supported by citation to Duits et al., 2015

claim: Patients suffering from anxiety-related disorders show a tendency of fear generalization to innocuous stimuli compared to healthy controls.
source: Important findings in the fear conditioning field include the deficient learning of the safety signal (CS−) during acquisition training, impaired extinction learning (Duits et al., 2015) and the tendency of fear generalization to innocuous stimuli (Cooper et al., 2022a) in patients suffering from anxiety-related disorders as compared to healthy controls.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cooper et al., 2022a

claim: Clinical and experimental research using fear conditioning paradigms have primarily focused on group-level, basic, general mechanisms.
source: To date, both clinical and experimental research using the fear conditioning paradigm have primarily focused on group-level, basic, general mechanisms such as the effect of experimental manipulations – which is important to investigate (Lonsdorf and Merz, 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lonsdorf and Merz, 2017b

claim: Successful clinical translation requires that both the experimental paradigm and the measures employed allow for individual-level predictions over and above prediction of group averages.
source: Successful clinical translation (e.g., 'Why do some individuals develop pathological anxiety while others do not?') and particularly treatment outcome prediction (e.g., 'Why do some patients benefit from treatment while others relapse?'), however, requires that both the experimental paradigm and the measures employed allow for individual-level predictions over and above prediction of group averages (Fröhner et al., 2019; Hedge et al., 2018; Lonsdorf and Merz, 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fröhner et al., 2019; Hedge et al., 2018; and Lonsdorf and Merz, 2017b

claim: A prerequisite for individual-level predictions is that the measures show stability within and reliable differences between individuals over time.
source: A prerequisite for this is that the measures show stability within and reliable differences between individuals over time.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the requirements for individual-level predictions

claim: Tackling clinical questions regarding individual-level predictions requires a shift toward and a validation of research methods tailored to individual differences.
source: Hence, tackling clinical questions regarding individual-level predictions of symptom development or treatment outcome requires a shift toward and a validation of research methods tailored to individual differences – such as a focus on measurement reliability (Zuo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zuo et al., 2019

claim: There is pronounced heterogeneity in symptom manifestation among individuals diagnosed with the same disorders.
source: This further relates to the pronounced heterogeneity in symptom manifestation among individuals diagnosed with the same disorders (e.g., post-traumatic stress disorder, PTSD, Galatzer-Levy and Bryant, 2013b) which cannot be captured in binary clinical diagnoses as two patients with for example a PTSD diagnosis may not share a single symptom (Galatzer-Levy and Bryant, 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Galatzer-Levy and Bryant, 2013b

claim: Two patients with a PTSD diagnosis may not share a single symptom.
source: This further relates to the pronounced heterogeneity in symptom manifestation among individuals diagnosed with the same disorders (e.g., post-traumatic stress disorder, PTSD, Galatzer-Levy and Bryant, 2013b) which cannot be captured in binary clinical diagnoses as two patients with for example a PTSD diagnosis may not share a single symptom (Galatzer-Levy and Bryant, 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Galatzer-Levy and Bryant, 2013b

claim: Measurement reliability has only recently gained momentum in experimental cognitive research.
source: Measurement reliability has only recently gained momentum in experimental cognitive research (Fröhner et al., 2019; Hedge et al., 2018; Zuo et al., 2019) and can be assessed through test–retest and longitudinal reliability (i.e., test–retest reliability over longer time intervals, typically assessed through e.g., intraclass correlation coefficients, ICCs, see Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fröhner et al., 2019; Hedge et al., 2018; and Zuo et al., 2019

claim: Longitudinal reliability has implications for the precision with which associations of one variable with another variable can be measured.
source: Importantly, longitudinal reliability (for definitions and terminology, see Table 1) also has implications for the precision with which associations of one variable (e.g., conditioned responding) with another (individual difference) variable can be measured because the correlation between those two variables cannot exceed the correlations within, that is the reliability, of these two variables (Spearman, 1910).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spearman, 1910

claim: The correlation between two variables cannot exceed the correlations within (the reliability of) these two variables.
source: Importantly, longitudinal reliability (for definitions and terminology, see Table 1) also has implications for the precision with which associations of one variable (e.g., conditioned responding) with another (individual difference) variable can be measured because the correlation between those two variables cannot exceed the correlations within, that is the reliability, of these two variables (Spearman, 1910).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spearman, 1910

claim: In fear conditioning research, little is known about longitudinal reliability at the individual level with time intervals ranging from 9 days to 8 months in prior work.
source: Yet, in fear conditioning research, surprisingly little is known about longitudinal reliability at the individual level with time intervals ranging from 9 days to 8 months in prior work (Supplementary file 1; Cooper et al., 2022b; Fredrikson et al., 1993; Ridderbusch et al., 2021; Torrents-Rodas et al., 2014; Zeidan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cooper et al., 2022b; Fredrikson et al., 1993; Ridderbusch et al., 2021; Torrents-Rodas et al., 2014; and Zeidan et al., 2012

claim: Individual-level longitudinal reliability of risk ratings, skin conductance responses, and fear potentiated startle was within the same range.
source: Generally (details in Supplementary file 1), individual-level longitudinal reliability of risk ratings, skin conductance responses (SCRs), and fear potentiated startle (FPS) was within the same range (Cooper et al., 2022b; Torrents-Rodas et al., 2014) whereas it was numerically somewhat lower for the BOLD response as compared to different rating types (Ridderbusch et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cooper et al., 2022b and Torrents-Rodas et al., 2014

claim: Individual-level longitudinal reliability was numerically somewhat lower for the BOLD response as compared to different rating types.
source: Generally (details in Supplementary file 1), individual-level longitudinal reliability of risk ratings, skin conductance responses (SCRs), and fear potentiated startle (FPS) was within the same range (Cooper et al., 2022b; Torrents-Rodas et al., 2014) whereas it was numerically somewhat lower for the BOLD response as compared to different rating types (Ridderbusch et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ridderbusch et al., 2021

claim: Longitudinal reliability at the individual level appeared higher for acquisition training than for extinction training.
source: Longitudinal reliability at the individual level appeared higher for acquisition training than for extinction training (SCRs: Fredrikson et al., 1993; Zeidan et al., 2012), but comparable to generalization (Cooper et al., 2022b; Torrents-Rodas et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fredrikson et al., 1993 and Zeidan et al., 2012

evidence: Supported by citations to Cooper et al., 2022b and Torrents-Rodas et al., 2014

source: Moreover, it appeared higher for extinction training than for reinstatement-test (for BOLD fMRI but not ratings: Ridderbusch et al., 2021) and higher for CS+ than CS− responses (SCRs: Fredrikson et al., 1993) and CS discrimination (ratings and BOLD fMRI: Ridderbusch et al., 2021; SCRs: Zeidan et al., 2012).

claim: No study to date has investigated longitudinal reliability at the group level in fear conditioning research.
source: Given that the predominance of research on group-level generic mechanisms in fear conditioning research, it is even more surprising that, to our knowledge, no study to date has investigated longitudinal reliability at the group level and only few studies have (Fredrikson et al., 1993) targeted internal consistency (i.e., the degree to which all test items capture the same construct, see Table 1).
evidence: Authors state this based on their knowledge of the literature

claim: The study reanalyzed data from 120 participants that underwent a differential fear conditioning paradigm twice 6 months apart.
source: With this pre-registered study, we follow the call for a stronger appreciation and more systematic investigations of measurement reliability (Zuo et al., 2019). We address longitudinal reliability and internal consistency as well as predictability of cross-phase responding in SCRs, fear ratings, and the BOLD response. For this purpose, we reanalyzed data from 120 participants that underwent a differential fear conditioning paradigm twice (at time points T0 and T1, 6 months apart) – with habituation and acquisition training on day 1 and extinction, reinstatement and reinstatement-test on day 2 to allow for fear memory consolidation prior to extinction.

claim: The work highlights the value of using multiple, more nuanced measures of reliability beyond traditional ICCs.

Our work allows for some initial recommendations and insights. First, we highlight the value of using multiple, more nuanced measures of reliability beyond traditional ICCs (i.e,. similarity, overlap, Fröhner et al., 2019) and second, the relation between number of trials and reliability in an experiment with a learning component (i.e., no increase in reliability with an increasing number of trials).
evidence: Based on the study's approach and findings with citation to Fröhner et al., 2019
